messages.subject: Re: Common Method Variance in Psychometrics
messages.body_plain:
Hi

To add to Ed's comments. It is good to separate 3 part of the process, model, inference, and estimation.
The model (like SEM) will have similar constraints/limitations in all conditions, because those characterictics of the model itself, like the issue you mention here
The inference is what framework is used to make probabilitic statements, like frequentist or bayesian
The estimation, are the algorithms to put the model and inference together, like MCMC in Bayesian or ML/WLS in frequentist

take care

On Tuesday, June 27, 2023 at 5:25:41 AM UTC+2 Ed Merkle wrote:
> I think that CMV would be a problem for Bayesian SEM whenever it is a problem for frequentist SEM. I am not completely familiar with all the procedures that you mention, and I don't immediately know of Bayesian applications to CMV. But the procedures seem to involve model comparisons, and it would be possible to use a Bayesian metric like LOO or WAIC to do the comparison of Bayesian models.
>
> Ed
>
>
> On Mon, 2023-06-26 at 04:31 -0700, Gokay Kirtil wrote:

> >
> > My question is,  in social sciences- psychometrics there is a threat of Common Method Variance (CMV) -therefore bias- if we're using a survey from the same response method. In SEM studies from Classical Test Theory, there are some procedural and statistical remedies regarding CMV. For example Harman's single factor test, marker variable method, measured or unmeasured latent method are few of them. These could be applied to check if we're under threat of CMV.
> >
> > Could we or should we also apply these in a Bayesian SEM ? If so how they should be reported ? are there any sources regarding this issue. Thats my point..
> >

> > **Understanding and managing the threat of common method bias: Detection, prevention and control (Kock et al, 2021)

Something like that below. If you need a mwe, let me know. This works in lavaan, though usually I need to fiddle with starting values. There is also more than one way to parameterize the model. Many thanks!

modcov2 <- "
# variances
X1 ~~ X1
X2 ~~ X2
X3 ~~ X3
X4 ~~ X4
X5 ~~ X5

# covariances
X1 ~~ c12*X2
X1 ~~ c13*X3
X1 ~~ c14*X4
X1 ~~ c15*X5
X2 ~~ c23*X3
X2 ~~ c24*X4
X2 ~~ c25*X5
X3 ~~ X4
X3 ~~ X5
X4 ~~ X5

# constraints
c13/c23 == c14/c24
c13/c23 == c15/c25

# alternative way to do it, but estimation difficulty in lavaan
#c13 == c14/c24*c23
#c13 == c15/c25*c23

# intercepts
X1 ~ 1
X2 ~ 1
X3 ~ 1
X4 ~ 1
X5 ~ 1

"

messages.subject: Re: question re: functions of parameters
messages.body_plain:
You should be able to do the "alternative parameterization" if you use JAGS for estimation (by adding the argument target="jags"). blavaan lags behind lavaan with these constraint specifications, and blavaan needs you to isolate one parameter on the lhs of the constraint.

For the default target="stan", only simple equality constraints are currently allowed. This is because the underlying Stan model is precompiled. If you really need the efficiency of Stan here, it may be possible to edit the underlying Stan model with a bit of work. But it would require more discussion/detail.

Ed

messages.subject: Re: question re: functions of parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carl,

I had a look at this and found that your error comes from the fact that both of the equality constraints have c13 on the left side of the equation. So I think "length > 1" says that it found two definitions of c13 and doesn't know which to use.

You can get a bit further by, say, putting c25 on the left side of the second constraint and moving c13 to the right. Then blavaan starts to run the model in JAGS but JAGS complains about "Invalid parent values". One issue there is that the c12-c25 parameters are correlations in blavaan, as opposed to covariances. This is because the residual covariance matrix in blavaan is decomposed as "SRS", where S is a diagonal matrix of SDs and R is the correlation matrix. But I think your constraints are actually about correlations because, if you write out the covariances and divide them, the constraints really say

r13/r23 == r14/r24

where, e.g., r13 is the correlation between X1 and X3. So I think you still end up with the same constraints as before, but then taking r13 = r14/r24 * r23 can push r13 above 1, which is impossible for a correlation, leading to problems in the model.

I wonder whether you might make progress by adding a latent variable to handle covariances, then maybe constraining loadings could indirectly get these constraints. Or you could make the constraint a bit more restrictive and say c13=c14=c15 and c23=c24=c25. But in general, I find constraints on covariances to be tricky.

Ed

> Julian,
>
> Thanks for the report. I can reproduce this message, and it is related to the posterior predictive p-value computations. I think it happens because you have 24 observations in the data, and 24 variables are included in the model. So there is a 24x24 covariance matrix that is being computed from 24 simulated observations, which leads to the positive definite problems. I would be mildly surprised if this previously ran without issue, but to avoid the message you could add
>
> test = "none"
>
> to your blavaan() command.
>
> It also looks like the default priors will not work well for your dataset, and perhaps the easiest thing to do is divide the entire dataset by 10. But, with only 24 observations, you probably want to give the priors good consideration because they will likely influence the posteriors.
>
> Hope it helps,
> Ed

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the report. This problem was because blavaan supplied bad starting values for correlation parameters. It is now fixed on github.

I also notice that you are using random intercepts. The github version now allows for random intercept models (using the "cluster" argument like lavaan), though they are still being tested and they also only work for complete data. If you try it, I would be interested to hear about problems.

Ed
